title: The US Just Approved a $428 Million Deal to Keep India's Apaches and Howitzers Running.
excerpt: Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and BAE Systems will sustain India's most critical American-made weapons platforms. The deal deepens a defence relationship that is no longer aspirational.
body:
The United States has approved a pair of defence support deals with India worth more than $428 million, covering sustainment services for the Indian Army's fleet of Apache attack helicopters and its M777 ultra-light howitzers. The approval, announced by the U.S. State Department, deepens the defence supply chain between the two countries at a moment when both are navigating the geopolitical fallout of the Iran conflict.

The Apache sustainment package is valued at approximately $198.2 million and covers AH-64E Apache helicopter support services, engineering and technical logistics, personnel training, and technical publications. The M777A2 Ultra-Light Howitzer support deal is worth around $230 million and includes spares, repair and return services, depot capability, and field service representative support.

Boeing and Lockheed Martin are the principal contractors for the Apache package. BAE Systems will handle the howitzer support.

## Not New Hardware, but Something More Important

The significance of this deal is not in the dollar figure — by the standards of major defence procurement, $428 million is modest. It is in what the deal represents: the deepening of India's operational dependency on American defence platforms and the corresponding American interest in keeping those systems running.

India operates 22 AH-64E Apache Guardian helicopters, acquired in a $3 billion deal signed in 2015. The Army's Apache fleet is deployed primarily along the western border and in forward positions near the Line of Actual Control with China. The M777 howitzers — 145 guns purchased from BAE Systems — are positioned in mountainous terrain along the northern border, where their light weight (4,200 kg) allows them to be airlifted by Chinook helicopters to positions that conventional artillery cannot reach.

Both platforms are critical to India's defence posture in contested theaters. Without sustained U.S. support — spare parts, training, software updates, technical assistance — their operational readiness degrades rapidly.

"This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by helping to strengthen the U.S.-Indian strategic relationship and to improve the security of a major defence partner," the State Department said.

## The Bigger Picture: India as a Defence Customer

India is one of the world's largest arms importers, spending tens of billions of dollars annually on military equipment. Historically, the bulk of India's defence imports came from Russia — a relationship that Washington has worked systematically to erode over the past decade through technology transfer agreements, joint exercises, and precisely this kind of sustainment deal that locks India into American supply chains.

The Apache and M777 deals are part of a broader pattern. India has purchased C-17 Globemaster transport aircraft, P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, MH-60R Seahawk helicopters, and Harpoon missiles from American manufacturers. Each purchase comes with a long tail of maintenance, upgrades, and training that generates recurring revenue for U.S. defence firms and deepens interoperability between the two militaries.

This is by design. The Pentagon has designated India a "Major Defence Partner" — a status that grants access to advanced technology and streamlined export approvals. The State Department noted in its announcement that India "will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces," a diplomatic way of saying that the Indian military's ability to operate American equipment is no longer in question.

## Why NRIs Should Follow This

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the defence relationship between Washington and New Delhi is both a source of strategic reassurance and a growing industry. Indian Americans work across the U.S. defence sector — at Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, and dozens of smaller contractors. Several Indian-origin executives hold senior positions in companies that directly benefit from these deals.

The defence relationship also serves as a geopolitical anchor. At a time when the Iran conflict has disrupted India's energy security and the trade relationship faces the overhang of Section 301 tariffs, the defence partnership provides continuity — a domain where the two governments are aligned regardless of who occupies the White House.

The Indian Air Force is expected to focus on two major procurement decisions in the coming months: the Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme, which will acquire 114 jets, and engine partnerships for the indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. Both decisions will further define whether India's defence future tilts toward American, European, or a mixed portfolio of suppliers.

For now, the Apache and M777 support deals are a reminder that the U.S.-India defence relationship is no longer aspirational. It is operational, institutional, and increasingly difficult to reverse.
